name: Car seats (if retained in HMTc scope)
category_name: Infant and Child Durable Goods and Textiles (Ages 0-5)
anchor: Total-content children's-product and surface-coating law (US CPSIA s.101 and 16 CFR 1303; Canada SOR/2018-83 and SOR/2016-193; EU REACH Annex XVII entry 23; Australian Customs (Prohibited Imports) Regulations 1956 Schedule 2 coating values) for durable goods and fasteners, and the EU REACH Annex XVII entry 72 Appendix 12 extraction limits for clothing, bibs and bedding.
native_basis: total element content of each accessible component material of the finished article as placed on market, expressed as mg/kg of the homogenised component (or of the dried non-volatile coating film for a coating component), determined by microwave-assisted acid digestion and ICP-MS. This is a CONTENT basis. It is not an element-migration or leachate basis (EN 71-3 / Directive 2009/48/EC, ASTM F963 soluble elements, EU 10/2011 specific migration into food) and it is not the REACH Annex XVII entry 72 after-extraction textile basis.
native_basis_label: total element content of the accessible component material (mg/kg of component; dried non-volatile film for coatings) — a content basis, not a migration or extraction basis
scope_note: Rear-facing, forward-facing, convertible and all-in-one child restraint systems and belt-positioning boosters, including the shell, harness, cover, foam and base. SCOPE FLAG, carried from the taxonomy row and not resolved here: a child restraint system is motor-vehicle equipment. Motor-vehicle equipment is excluded from the US Consumer Product Safety Act definition of a consumer product by the motor-vehicle-equipment exclusion in 15 U.S.C. 2052(a)(5), the same definitional paragraph the register cites for the cosmetics, drugs and devices exclusions, so the CPSIA s.101 children's-product lead limit and 16 CFR 1303 do not reach it directly, and its safety performance is set by FMVSS 213 rather than by the CPSC; the Canadian position is analogous, restraint systems being regulated under motor-vehicle restraint-system law. FMVSS 213 sets no heavy-metal limit of any kind. This row is therefore built as a DISCLOSED READ-ACROSS for lead rather than as a direct government limit, and whether the category is retained in HMTc scope at all remains a Step 0 question for the category lock. Where the article incorporates a component that is itself a toy — an activity bar, play panel, toy tray, suspended rattle or teether attached to the frame — that component is separately in scope of Directive 2009/48/EC and must meet the EN 71-3 element-migration limits for its own material category (Category I dry/brittle/powder-like/pliable, Category II liquid or sticky, Category III scraped-off; rigid moulded plastic and cured paint on such a component are Category III). Those are 0.07 M HCl leachate limits in a different basis from this row and are recorded as a companion conformity obligation, never as this row's published ceiling. Such a toy component is certified under Category 21 (Children's Toys, Arts, and Crafts) on the EN 71-3 material category appropriate to it, and is not homogenised into an accessible-component sample on this row. One consequence of that scope flag is worked through consistently across every cell of this record. The instruments applied here by DISCLOSED READ-ACROSS are the consumer-product-safety instruments whose reach a restraint system escapes: Canada SOR/2018-83 on lead, Canada SOR/2016-193 on mercury, and the Australian Customs (Prohibited Imports) Regulations 1956 Schedule 2 coated-toy values on arsenic, cadmium and chromium. REACH Annex XVII is a different kind of instrument — a restriction on the manufacture, placing on the market and use of substances in articles generally, rather than a consumer-product-safety statute — so its entry 23 cadmium restriction on articles produced from the listed synthetic organic polymers and its entry 47 hexavalent-chromium restriction on skin-contact leather are not displaced by the motor-vehicle-equipment point and bind the corresponding materials of a restraint system on their own terms. Where such a cell is nonetheless tagged read-across, that is because the published value comes from an analogous article class or is extended article-wide, not because REACH is being treated as inapplicable.
material: moulded polypropylene and expanded polystyrene or polypropylene shell and energy-absorbing foam, polyester harness webbing and cover fabric, steel reinforcement and belt-path hardware, moulded acetal and nylon buckle and chest clip, and printed labels and warning decals
components: shell and base polymer; energy-absorbing EPS or EPP foam; cover fabric, its coating or lamination, and its print; harness webbing; buckle body, chest clip and tongue; steel reinforcement, LATCH or ISOFIX connector and its plating; metal fasteners; applied decals, warning labels and printed graphics — each sampled and digested as a distinct homogeneous component, with the buckle, chest clip, harness webbing and cover surface within the child's mouthing zone sampled first
basis_guard: ^(?!.*(migration|migratable|soluble|bioavailable|after extraction|leachate|as consumed|as sold|edible|muscle meat|wet weight|product as placed on market|portion ordinarily consumed))(?=.*(content|paint|surface coating|coating material|plastic material|leather|percent by weight|homogeneous material))
basis_guard_note: Drawn at the boundary of the TOTAL-CONTENT family. It admits only register rows whose basis is the mass fraction of the element in a homogenised component, coating film, plastic material or metal part, and rejects every leachate/transfer basis: EN 71-3 / Directive 2009/48/EC toy migration, ASTM F963 and NOM-252 soluble/bioavailable elements, GB 21027 migratable content, EU 10/2011 specific migration into food, the REACH Annex XVII entry 72 after-extraction textile basis, and all dietary wet-weight and as-consumed food maximum levels. A migration number is a different measured quantity from a content number and must never be published as one; if a named anchor drifts across the boundary the cell resolves to a GAP and the build fails.
method: HMTc Method v2.0 (government-limit-only): the strictest applicable maximum set by a credible sovereign government for this exact product form in the row's declared native basis; a disclosed read-across from the nearest applicable sovereign cell where the exact cell is unregulated; a substantiated not-material determination where the analyte is a species bounded by a published parent; and a control with a named reference method where neither a sovereign value nor a supportable read-across exists. Never occurrence-derived.

Pb.source_scope: accessible parts of consumer products containing lead, including mouth-contact products, child clothing/accessories, child learning/play products, certain child printed products, and products for sleep, relaxation, hygiene, carrying, or transport of children under four
Pb.label: Canada SOR/2018-83 s.2(1): 90 mg/kg total lead in each accessible part of a consumer product for the sleep, relaxation, hygiene, carrying or transport of a child under four, read across to a child restraint system.
Pb.substantiation: The exact cell is unregulated for lead. A child restraint system is motor-vehicle equipment, excluded from the US Consumer Product Safety Act definition of a consumer product by the motor-vehicle-equipment exclusion in 15 U.S.C. 2052(a)(5), so neither CPSIA s.101 (100 mg/kg substrate) nor 16 CFR 1303 (90 mg/kg surface coating) reaches it directly; FMVSS 213, the instrument that does govern it, sets no heavy-metal limit. Rather than assert a direct government limit that does not apply, HMTc reads across the 90 mg/kg accessible-part lead limit from the nearest applicable sovereign article class — consumer products for the carrying and transport of children under four — and applies it to every accessible component of the restraint. The read-across is disclosed on the record and the value is the same 90 mg/kg published on every other row in this category, so a restraint system is held to the children's-product ceiling even though the children's-product statute does not reach it. Companion sub-national obligations, disclosed and not adopted as the anchor: the Washington Children's Safe Product Act (register rows wa_cspa2008_pb_childrens_products_90ppm, s.3(1)(a), and wa_cspa2008_cd_childrens_products_40ppm, s.3(1)(b)) prohibits lead above 90 mg/kg and cadmium above 40 mg/kg in a children's product or product component, and Minnesota Statutes 325E.3892 prohibits lead above 90 mg/kg and cadmium above 75 mg/kg in covered consumer products. Both are stricter than the adopted cadmium anchor. Neither is selected here because each statute's own product definition is narrower than the CPSIA 'children's product' definition and the register carries only the phrases 'children's products and product components covered by the Washington Children's Safe Product Act' and 'covered consumer products and product components listed in Minnesota Statutes section 325E.3892, subject to exceptions', which do not establish whether this product form is inside the covered list. Applicability to the exact cell cannot be resolved from the register, so the rows are published as jurisdiction-specific companion obligations and logged as register gaps for scope-resolved re-ingest rather than selected as the HMTc value.

Cd.label: Strictest applicable total-content cadmium limit among this article's principal components: the Australian Customs (Prohibited Imports) Regulations 1956 Schedule 2 coating value of 75 mg/kg on the non-volatile content of the coating material, read across from coated toys to the coated components of this durable good. HMTc applies the strictest component value article-wide, which is stricter than each component's own limit and never looser.
Cd.substantiation: All three candidates are TOTAL-CONTENT limits, so the strictest-of-components selection compares like with like. The EU REACH Annex XVII entry 23 plastic-material value (100 mg/kg) binds the article's moulded polymer components DIRECTLY; the EU painted-article value (1 000 mg/kg) binds its paint layer directly; the Australian coating value (75 mg/kg) is scoped to toys coated with a material and is therefore READ ACROSS to the coatings of a child restraint system or booster car seat, which is not a toy but is a coated article for the same child, in the same mouthing and handling contact. Because the read-across value is the strictest of the three it becomes the published ceiling and is applied to every accessible component, including the polymer components whose own direct limit is 100 mg/kg — deliberate over-compliance, disclosed rather than silent. Companion sub-national obligations, disclosed and not adopted as the anchor: the Washington Children's Safe Product Act (register rows wa_cspa2008_pb_childrens_products_90ppm, s.3(1)(a), and wa_cspa2008_cd_childrens_products_40ppm, s.3(1)(b)) prohibits lead above 90 mg/kg and cadmium above 40 mg/kg in a children's product or product component, and Minnesota Statutes 325E.3892 prohibits lead above 90 mg/kg and cadmium above 75 mg/kg in covered consumer products. Both are stricter than the adopted cadmium anchor. Neither is selected here because each statute's own product definition is narrower than the CPSIA 'children's product' definition and the register carries only the phrases 'children's products and product components covered by the Washington Children's Safe Product Act' and 'covered consumer products and product components listed in Minnesota Statutes section 325E.3892, subject to exceptions', which do not establish whether this product form is inside the covered list. Applicability to the exact cell cannot be resolved from the register, so the rows are published as jurisdiction-specific companion obligations and logged as register gaps for scope-resolved re-ingest rather than selected as the HMTc value. COMPLIANCE OBLIGATION, stated so this record cannot be read as certifying a value the licensee cannot lawfully sell. The cadmium ceiling published on this row is 75 mg/kg, which sits ABOVE the Washington Children's Safe Product Act prohibition on cadmium exceeding 40 mg/kg in a children's product or product component (register row wa_cspa2008_cd_childrens_products_40ppm, s.3(1)(b); the Act is codified in Washington's RCW chapter 70A.430). That Act's own definition of a children's product enumerates car seats, products designed to help a child sleep, relax or feed, and products worn as clothing by children, which reaches most of the forms certified on this row. A lot returning cadmium above 40 mg/kg would therefore conform to the HMTc ceiling and still be unlawful to sell in Washington. Any such result is escalated as a jurisdiction-specific regulatory hard stop under the HMTc legal-violation rule and is never certified without that qualification, pending scope-resolved re-ingest of the Washington row through the verified regulatory-fetch pathway. The Minnesota cadmium value (75 mg/kg, register row mn_325e3892_2025_cd_covered_consumer_products_75ppm) equals the published ceiling rather than undercutting it, so a lot conforming here conforms there. Where the article incorporates a battery or a battery-powered module — a vibration unit, a sound or music module, a night light, a powered mobile or a powered rocker — the battery is a distinct regulated article with its own instrument, and its limits are not this row's. Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 restricts cadmium in a portable battery whether or not incorporated into an appliance (register row eu_batteries_2023_cd_portable_batteries_20000, 20 mg/kg) and mercury in a battery (register row eu_batteries_2023_thg_batteries_5000, 5 mg/kg), both expressed on the weight of the battery. Both are stricter than the values published here and both are recorded as companion obligations on the battery in a battery-by-weight basis; the battery is never homogenised into an accessible-component sample and its instrument is never merged into this row's component-content ceiling. Where the article carries no battery and no powered module the obligation does not arise.

tAs.label: Australian Customs (Prohibited Imports) Regulations 1956 Schedule 2 item 2: 25 mg/kg arsenic in the non-volatile content of coating material on a coated toy, read across to the coatings and coated components of this durable good.
tAs.substantiation: This is the only TOTAL-CONTENT arsenic maximum in the register that reaches a coated children's article. It is an unspeciated arsenic value (the register records that arsenic, mercury and chromium are unspecified species in this instrument and are mapped per ingest policy), so it is published on the tAs cell and never on iAs. The read-across is disclosed: the instrument's own scope is 'toys coated with a material' and a child restraint system or booster car seat is not a toy, but it is a coated article placed in the same child's hands and mouth, and no credible sovereign sets an arsenic content maximum for the exact cell. The ASTM F963 arsenic value (25 mg/kg) is numerically identical but sits in a soluble-element leachate basis and is excluded by this row's basis guard; the EN 71-3 Category III arsenic migration value (47 mg/kg) is likewise a leachate limit and is looser.

iAs.rationale: No credible sovereign publishes an inorganic-arsenic limit for a child restraint system or booster car seat; every arsenic instrument that reaches this category regulates the total element (the Australian coating-content limit adopted for the tAs cell is explicitly an unspeciated arsenic value, and REACH Annex XVII entry 72 Appendix 12 likewise limits arsenic compounds expressed as As metal). Inorganic arsenic is nevertheless NOT declared not-material here, because residual arsenic in dyestuff and pigment feedstocks used on the cover fabric and printed labels, and arsenic carried in recycled-content polymer feedstock is a real inorganic-arsenic pathway in this article class and a not-material determination would be an affirmative claim the material contradicts. The species is therefore held under mandatory analytical control, bounded above by the published total-arsenic ceiling.
iAs.reference_method: Mandatory total-arsenic content screen on every accessible component by microwave-assisted acid digestion and ICP-MS, with reflex inorganic-arsenic speciation by HPLC-ICP-MS (arsenite and arsenate, after a speciation-preserving extraction) on any component returning total arsenic above the reporting limit. Preservative-treated timber, arsenical pigments and recycled-content polymers are sampled as distinct components. Results are dispositioned under the HMTc control-and-escalation rule; inorganic arsenic can never exceed the published total-arsenic ceiling by identity.

tHg.basis: total mercury content of the accessible component material and of the dried non-volatile coating film (mg/kg) — the sovereign value is written for surface coating material and is extended by disclosed read-across, not asserted as direct alignment
tHg.label: Canada Surface Coating Materials Regulations SOR/2016-193 s.5 (10 mg/kg total mercury in a dried sample of surface coating material), read across to the dried applied film on a child restraint system or booster car seat and then extended article-wide to every accessible component as disclosed over-compliance.
tHg.substantiation: The published value is 10 mg/kg, but it is reached by DISCLOSED READ-ACROSS and not by direct regulatory alignment, because the instrument's scope is narrower than the cell this row publishes. Canada SOR/2016-193 s.5 sets 10 mg/kg total mercury in a dried sample of SURFACE COATING MATERIAL; the register's product_scope for that row is 'surface coating material', which is the coating substance itself. The same instrument distinguishes that scope from the applied-coating scope — its s.6 reaches a sticker, film or surface coating material applied to accessible parts of furniture and products for children (register row ca_sor2016_193_pb_applied_stickers_films_coatings_90000) — and s.6 is lead-only, with no mercury analogue anywhere in the register. Publishing s.5 as a DIRECT sovereign ceiling for the homogenised wood, steel tube, moulded polymer, foam and textile of a child restraint system or booster car seat would therefore over-read the instrument, which is the defect this cell was rebuilt to remove. HMTc reaches the value in two disclosed steps instead. Step one reads s.5 across from the coating material as such to the dried applied film on the finished article; the nearest sovereign instrument written in exactly that applied-coating scope is Canada Toys Regulations SOR/2011-17 s.23(1)(c) (register row ca_sor2011_17_thg_accessible_toy_coating_10), which sets the same 10 mg/kg for total mercury in surface coating materials applied to accessible parts of a child's article, so step one lands on a number a sovereign has already written for an applied coating on a children's product. Step two extends that same 10 mg/kg to every accessible component of a child restraint system or booster car seat, which no sovereign requires and which HMTc adopts as deliberate over-compliance, disclosed here rather than applied silently. At 10 mg/kg the value is six times stricter than the Australian toy-coating mercury value (60 mg/kg, register row au_customs_1956_thg_toys_coating_60mgkg). The EN 71-3 Category III scraped-off-material total-mercury migration value (94 mg/kg, register row eu_2009_48_cat3_thg_toy_migration) measures transfer rather than content, is looser, and is excluded by this row's basis guard. A second and independent ground, recorded here so this record takes ONE consistent position across all of its cells: a child restraint system is motor-vehicle equipment, excluded from the US Consumer Product Safety Act definition of a consumer product by the motor-vehicle-equipment exclusion in 15 U.S.C. 2052(a)(5), and the Canadian position is analogous, restraint systems and booster seats being regulated under motor-vehicle restraint-system law rather than under consumer-product law. Consumer-product-family instruments are therefore applied to this article by disclosed read-across and never as direct alignment — SOR/2018-83 on the lead cell and SOR/2016-193 here. The earlier version of this record asserted direct regulatory alignment for mercury while simultaneously grounding the lead read-across on the proposition that consumer-product law does not reach a restraint system; those two statements could not both be true, and the read-across position is the one adopted.

MeHg.rationale: Methylmercury is a marine-bioaccumulation species. It has no formation route and no established industrial source in a child restraint system or booster car seat: the mercury that can occur here comes from pigment, catalyst and preservative residues in coatings, polymers and dyestuffs, all of which are inorganic or aryl-mercury chemistries, and organomercury fungicides in these materials have been withdrawn across every jurisdiction checked. Every sovereign mercury instrument that reaches this article class is written on TOTAL mercury; not one sets a methylmercury value for an article, a coating or a textile. Methylmercury is a proper subset of total mercury by identity, so the 10 mg/kg total-mercury ceiling published on this row by disclosed read-across bounds it absolutely and a separate methylmercury ceiling would add no protection.
MeHg.reference_method: Total-mercury content screen by microwave-assisted acid digestion with CV-AFS or ICP-MS on every accessible component, with reflex methylmercury speciation by GC-ICP-MS reserved for any component that both exceeds the total-mercury reporting limit and carries a declared organomercury input. No routine methylmercury determination is required.
MeHg.substantiation: Bounded by the total-mercury cell on this same row, which publishes 10 mg/kg by disclosed read-across from Canada SOR/2016-193 s.5, landing on the value Canada SOR/2011-17 s.23(1)(c) writes for a coating applied to an accessible part of a child's article. The bound is therefore against a real, published, sovereign-derived ceiling carried on this record, not against an assertion that mercury is absent. It is described here as a read-across and not as a direct alignment because that is what the total-mercury cell on this record is.
MeHg.regulatory_basis: No credible sovereign sets a methylmercury limit for an article, a surface coating or a textile. The mercury instruments that reach this category are Canada SOR/2016-193 s.5 (10 mg/kg total mercury in a dried sample of surface coating material), Canada SOR/2011-17 s.23(1)(c) (10 mg/kg total mercury in accessible toy coatings), the Australian Customs (Prohibited Imports) Regulations 1956 Schedule 2 toy-coating value (60 mg/kg, unspeciated) and Directive 2009/48/EC Annex II Part III (total-mercury migration) — all total-element.
MeHg.jurisdictions_checked: EU (REACH Annex XVII entries 23, 27, 47, 63, 72; Directive 2009/48/EC; Directive 2011/65/EU RoHS; Regulation 10/2011), US (CPSIA s.101, 16 CFR 1303, ASTM F963 via CPSIA s.106), Canada (SOR/2016-193, SOR/2018-82, SOR/2018-83, SOR/2011-17), Australia (Customs (Prohibited Imports) Regulations 1956 Schedule 2), UK, Codex — register-checked, no methylmercury row for any article, coating or textile scope.

Ni.rationale: No credible sovereign publishes a nickel CONTENT maximum for a child restraint system or booster car seat. The governing instrument for the actual hazard — allergic contact dermatitis from prolonged skin contact with buckle tongues, chest clips, LATCH and ISOFIX connectors, plated fasteners and belt-path hardware — is the REACH Annex XVII entry 27 nickel-release restriction, which is expressed as an areal release rate (µg/cm² per week) and therefore cannot be expressed in this register's µg/kg content unit; it is not present in the register in any form. The EN 71-3 toy nickel migration values and the EU 10/2011 nickel specific-migration value both sit in leachate bases outside this row's native basis. No number is invented: the cell is held under mandatory analytical control.
Ni.reference_method: Mandatory total-nickel content analysis of every accessible metal, plated and alloy component by microwave-assisted acid digestion and ICP-MS, plus EN 1811 nickel-release testing (with EN 12472 wear-and-corrosion pre-treatment for coated or plated parts) on every component in prolonged skin contact, dispositioned against the release criterion in the REACH Annex XVII entry 27 restriction as a companion conformity obligation. That criterion's numeric value is deliberately NOT reproduced here: the restriction is absent from data/evidence/regulatory_limits.csv, and this standard quotes no number that is not carried by a named register row. The criterion is applied from the instrument text at audit and is logged as a register gap for ingest through the verified regulatory-fetch pathway. Any component exceeding the release criterion, or any total-nickel result that is an outlier against the supplier's own qualification data, triggers supplier corrective action under the HMTc control-and-escalation rule.

Sn.rationale: No credible sovereign publishes a total-tin content maximum for a child restraint system or booster car seat. The instrument that does reach this article class — REACH Annex XVII entry 20, which covers textile articles intended to come into contact with the skin, childcare articles and other consumer articles in skin contact — restricts ORGANOTIN (dibutyltin and dioctyltin) expressed as tin at 0.1 % by weight. Organotin expressed as tin is a different measurand from total tin: publishing 1 000 mg/kg as this row's total-tin ceiling would pass off a speciated restriction as a total-element limit. The organotin restriction is therefore carried as a companion obligation and no total-tin number is invented. This row DOES read a value across for hexavalent chromium, and the difference is principled rather than convenient: the chromium read-across crosses only a MATERIAL boundary while holding the analyte and the basis fixed, whereas an organotin read-across would cross an ANALYTE boundary, publishing a speciated restriction as a total-element ceiling. A material boundary can be crossed with disclosure; an analyte boundary cannot be crossed at all.
Sn.reference_method: Mandatory total-tin content analysis by microwave-assisted acid digestion and ICP-MS, with reflex organotin speciation by GC-ICP-MS (dibutyltin, dioctyltin, tributyltin, triphenyltin) on any component returning total tin above the reporting limit. Speciated results are dispositioned against the REACH Annex XVII entry 20 0.1 %-as-tin companion criterion; total-tin results are dispositioned under the HMTc control-and-escalation rule against the tightest available supplier qualification context.

Al.rationale: No credible sovereign publishes an aluminium content maximum for a child restraint system or booster car seat. Aluminium is a structural alloy in this category — frames, tubing, folding mechanisms, rivets and buckle bodies are routinely aluminium by design — so a content ceiling on the homogenised component is not a meaningful contamination control and no sovereign has set one. The EN 71-3 Category III aluminium migration value (28 130 mg/kg) and the EU 10/2011 aluminium specific-migration value (1 mg/kg into food) are leachate limits in other bases and are not read across into a content ceiling. No number is invented.
Al.reference_method: Mandatory total-aluminium content analysis by microwave-assisted acid digestion and ICP-MS on every non-structural accessible component (coatings, plastics, textiles, foams, printed decals), with structural aluminium alloy components identified and dispositioned by declared alloy specification rather than by a contamination ceiling. Aluminium detected in a component whose declared composition contains no aluminium is treated as a contamination signal and escalated to supplier corrective action.

Cr.screen_note: Total chromium is a screen cell, not a firm protective ceiling: the measured total is dominated by trivalent chromium from tanning agents, chromium(III) pigments and stainless-steel alloy, while the health-relevant species is Cr(VI). A total-chromium result at or below 60 mg/kg does not by itself demonstrate Cr(VI) compliance, and a total-chromium detection is the trigger for the Cr(VI) determination on this same row.
Cr.basis: total chromium content of the coating material and of the accessible component (mg/kg)
Cr.label: Australian Customs (Prohibited Imports) Regulations 1956 Schedule 2 item 2: 60 mg/kg chromium in the non-volatile content of coating material on a coated toy, read across to the coatings and coated components of this durable good. Reported as a SCREEN.
Cr.substantiation: The instrument records chromium as an unspecified species and the register maps it to total chromium. Total chromium in these materials is dominated by benign trivalent chromium — chrome-tanned leather trim, chromium(III) oxide pigments, stainless-steel alloy — so the value is recorded as a screen and is not treated as a standalone protective ceiling. The health-relevant species is Cr(VI), which is dispositioned on this row's Cr-VI control with the REACH Annex XVII entry 47 leather limit as a binding companion. The ASTM F963 total-chromium value (60 mg/kg) is numerically identical but sits in a soluble-element leachate basis and is excluded by this row's basis guard.

Cr-VI.binding_control: Determined by ISO 17075-1/-2 on every leather and leather-containing component, and by alkaline digestion with ion chromatography and post-column derivatisation (US EPA 3060A / 7199 approach) on chromate-pigmented coatings, chromate conversion coatings and plated metal parts. A leather component above the published value is a direct breach of REACH Annex XVII entry 47; a non-leather component above it breaches the read-across ceiling and triggers supplier corrective action and substitution to trivalent-chromium or chromium-free passivation.
Cr-VI.basis: hexavalent chromium content on the total dry weight of the component (mg/kg) — leather, coating film, or plated and conversion-coated metal part
Cr-VI.source_scope: leather articles and articles containing leather parts coming into contact with the skin
Cr-VI.label: EU REACH Annex XVII entry 47 paragraphs 5 and 6 (Regulation (EU) No 301/2014): 3 mg/kg hexavalent chromium on the total dry weight of leather, for leather articles and articles containing leather parts coming into contact with the skin. Applied article-wide.
Cr-VI.substantiation: This is the only hexavalent-chromium CONTENT limit in the register that reaches a skin-contact article, and it binds DIRECTLY wherever a child restraint system or booster car seat carries a leather part in skin contact — a leather handlebar or bumper-bar wrap, a harness pad, a leather trim panel or a leather pull tab. For the article's non-leather Cr(VI) pathways — chromate-pigmented coatings, chromate conversion coatings and hexavalent chrome plating on metal parts — no sovereign sets a content maximum, so the 3 mg/kg value is READ ACROSS to them and applied article-wide. The read-across is disclosed and is argued from the material and the contact, not from convenience: it keeps the SAME analyte (Cr(VI) specifically, not total chromium) and the SAME basis (mg/kg of the component's dry mass), and crosses only a material boundary, from chrome-tanned leather to a chromate-pigmented or chromate-passivated surface. The hazard is identical (Cr(VI) skin sensitisation) and the route is identical (dermal transfer under sweat from a surface held against the child), which is exactly why entry 47 was written for skin-contact leather in the first place. Applying it article-wide is deliberate over-compliance and is the same rule this row applies to lead (90 mg/kg applied to a substrate whose own US limit is 100 mg/kg) and to cadmium (75 mg/kg applied to polymer components whose own EU limit is 100 mg/kg); declining to extend it to Cr(VI), the analyte where compliance costs a supplier a change of passivation chemistry, would be selective over-compliance and is not done. The EU RoHS 0.1 % homogeneous-material Cr(VI) value is scoped to electrical and electronic equipment and is over three hundred times more permissive, so it is not used as the read-across source. The EN 71-3 Category I and II Cr(VI) migration values are numerically lower but are leachate limits measuring transfer rather than content, and are excluded by this row's basis guard.
